conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/name: The Shimabara Rebellion of Japanese Christians
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/religionRo: The Tokugawa regime presented the rising as a Christian rebellion, and it used Christian banners, slogans and a messianic youth leader in regions that had been heavily Catholic before the ban of 1614. Many earlier historians, however, treated it chiefly as a peasant revolt against crushing taxation, famine and brutal collection by the daimyo Matsukura Katsuie and Terazawa Katataka, joined by masterless samurai of the former Christian lords Arima and Konishi. Recent Japanese scholarship (for example Kanda Chisato and Ōhashi Yukihiro) has re-emphasised its religious, millenarian character: many former apostates publicly returned to Christianity, non-Christian villagers were pressed to convert, and temples and shrines were burned. Most historians now see an inseparable fusion of economic desperation and Christian hope.
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/sides/0/fa: Kirishitan (Japanese Catholic, many returned apostates), with non-Christian peasants
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/sides/1/na: Tokugawa shogunate and the Kyushu daimyo
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/sides/2/na: Dutch East India Company (in support of the shogunate)
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/summary: A rising of peasants, fishermen and masterless samurai in the formerly Christian districts of Shimabara and Amakusa in western Kyushu, led in name by the teenage Amakusa Shirō and fought under Catholic banners. After defeating the first assaults, some 27,000 or more rebels, including women and children, were besieged in the ruined Hara Castle and killed almost to the last person in April 1638. The rebellion confirmed the shogunate's resolve to eradicate Christianity and close Japan to the Portuguese.
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/story:
Catholicism had spread rapidly in Kyushu after Francis Xavier's arrival in 1549. The Shimabara peninsula was ruled by the Christian daimyo Arima Harunobu and the Amakusa islands by the Christian general Konishi Yukinaga, and by 1600 their lands were among the most Christian regions of Asia. After Konishi's execution in 1600 and Arima's fall in 1612, new lords took over: the Matsukura family in Shimabara and the Terazawa in Amakusa. The Tokugawa ban on Christianity in 1614 expelled missionaries and began decades of persecution: the 'Great Martyrdom' of Nagasaki in 1622, the use of fumie (images to be trampled) and, around Shimabara, the torture of Christians in the boiling springs of Mount Unzen under Matsukura Shigemasa from 1627.

Matsukura Katsuie, who inherited Shimabara in 1630, imposed taxes far beyond the domain's real yield to pay for castle building and service to the shogun. Peasants who failed to pay were tortured, and accounts tell of men dressed in straw raincoats set alight (the 'mino odori', straw-coat dance) and of family members held hostage. Several years of poor harvests and famine in the mid-1630s pushed villages beyond endurance. At the same time rumours spread of a prophecy attributed to a missionary expelled a quarter of a century earlier, that a heavenly youth would appear amid portents to save the Christians. Many villagers identified this figure with Masuda Shirō, the sixteen-year-old son of a former Konishi retainer, credited with miracles.

In December 1637 (the tenth month of Kan'ei 14) villagers in Arima killed a local official who had broken up a Christian gathering and destroyed a sacred image. The rising spread rapidly through southern Shimabara: rebels killed officials and Buddhist priests, burned temples and shrines and besieged Shimabara Castle without success. Across the water, Amakusa villagers rose, defeated Terazawa troops and besieged Tomioka Castle, again without taking it. Early in 1638 the insurgents of both regions gathered in Hara Castle, an abandoned Arima fortress on cliffs overlooking the Ariake Sea, which they repaired and fortified. Estimates of the number inside range from about 27,000 to 37,000 men, women and children.

The shogunate sent Itakura Shigemasa to command the Kyushu domains. His assaults failed, and in a final attack on the first day of the new year (February 1638) he was killed with thousands of his men. Matsudaira Nobutsuna, a senior councillor, then took command of an army that grew to over 120,000. He ordered a blockade, siege works and mining, and asked the Dutch at Hirado for help: the ship de Ryp under Nicolaes Couckebacker bombarded the castle for about two weeks, firing several hundred rounds. The Dutch participation, Protestant Europeans firing on Japanese Catholics, was remembered with bitterness by Catholic writers and with some embarrassment by the Dutch themselves.

By April the defenders were starving; captured rebels were found with only seaweed and leaves in their stomachs. On 12 April 1638 (the 28th day of the second month) the shogunal army stormed the castle. The defenders resisted for two days, and virtually all were then killed, including women and children; the buildings were burned and the castle later demolished. Amakusa Shirō's head was displayed in Nagasaki. The painter Yamada Emosaku, who had secretly corresponded with the besiegers, was reportedly the only notable survivor.

The aftermath was severe. Matsukura Katsuie was condemned and beheaded in 1638, the only daimyo executed in this way in the Edo period, and Terazawa lost Amakusa. The shogunate concluded that Portuguese missionaries and traders were a permanent danger: in 1639 it expelled the Portuguese, and in 1641 the Dutch were confined to the artificial island of Dejima in Nagasaki harbour. The depopulated peninsula was resettled with migrants from other regions. Every household was required to register with a Buddhist temple and certify annually that it was not Christian, informers were rewarded, and the 'closed country' policy remained in force until the 1850s.

Christianity survived only in secret among the Kakure Kirishitan of the Nagasaki and Gotō regions, who passed on prayers and rites without priests for over two centuries. In modern Japan Amakusa Shirō became a romantic, sometimes nationalist, hero of resistance. The Catholic Church has not counted the dead of Hara Castle among the beatified martyrs of Japan, because they took up arms, though many Japanese Catholics remember them with sympathy.
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/nameOfGod: The rebels marched under Christian banners and cried 'Jesus', 'Maria' and 'Santiago'. A surviving banner, attributed to Amakusa Shirō and now in the Amakusa Christian Museum, shows two angels adoring a chalice and host beneath the Portuguese inscription 'Louvado seja o Santíssimo Sacramento' ('Praised be the Most Holy Sacrament'). Shirō was revered as the heaven-sent youth of prophecy, and rebel letters thrown into the besiegers' camp declared that they fought for their faith and that the next world mattered more than this one. Apostates were urged to return to the faith and non-Christians were pressed to convert. The shogunate in turn condemned Christianity as an 'evil teaching' (jakyō) that made subjects disloyal, and used the rebellion to justify the systematic eradication of the faith.
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/religiousC: The 1614 ban and the persecution of Christians, including torture at the Unzen hot springs, fell especially hard on the formerly Christian domains of Shimabara and Amakusa.
Many who had apostatised under pressure publicly returned to Christianity, and the rising became a collective act of repentance and faith.
A prophecy of a heaven-sent youth who would save the Christians focused hopes on Amakusa Shirō and gave the revolt a millenarian character.
Without priests since 1614, lay confraternities had maintained Christian networks that could quickly mobilise villages.
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/otherCause: Matsukura Katsuie and Terazawa Katataka imposed taxes far beyond what their lands could bear and enforced them with torture.
Famine and crop failures in the mid-1630s left many villages starving.
Masterless samurai of the dispossessed Arima and Konishi houses provided military leadership and resented the new lords.
Local grievances against officials and the strains of the new Tokugawa order on peripheral Kyushu communities.
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/triggers/0: The killing of a local official in Arima village in December 1637 after he broke up a Christian assembly and destroyed a sacred image.
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/triggers/1: Rumours that the heaven-sent youth had appeared in the person of Amakusa Shirō.
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/triggers/2: The rising of the Amakusa villagers against the Terazawa administration days later, which turned a local revolt into a regional war.
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/timeline/0: Francis Xavier arrives in Kagoshima; Catholicism later spreads widely in Kyushu.
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/timeline/1: Execution of the Christian daimyo Konishi Yukinaga; Amakusa passes to the Terazawa.
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/timeline/2: The Tokugawa shogunate bans Christianity and expels missionaries.
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/timeline/3: Great Martyrdom of Nagasaki: 55 Christians executed.
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/timeline/4: Torture of Christians at the Unzen hot springs begins under Matsukura Shigemasa.
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/timeline/5: Rising breaks out in Shimabara and Amakusa; sieges of Shimabara and Tomioka castles fail.
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/timeline/6: Rebels occupy Hara Castle; Itakura Shigemasa is killed; Dutch bombardment; Hara falls on 12 April and the defenders are massacred.
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/timeline/7: Matsukura Katsuie is executed for misgovernment.
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/timeline/8: The Portuguese are expelled from Japan.
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/timeline/9: The Dutch are confined to Dejima; temple registration is tightened.
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/timeline/1: Edicts against Christianity are finally removed.
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/keyPeople/: Charismatic youth leader of the rebellion
Baptised as Jerónimo, he was hailed as the prophesied heavenly youth and became the symbolic head of the rising, while experienced rōnin directed its military operations.
Killed when Hara Castle fell; his head was displayed at Nagasaki. He became a legendary figure in Japanese culture.
His crushing taxes and cruel enforcement, together with persecution of Christians, provoked the revolt.
Condemned by the shogunate and beheaded in 1638.
First shogunal commander against the rebels
Led the early assaults on Hara Castle, which failed with heavy losses.
Killed in the attack of February 1638.
Senior councillor (rōjū) and commander of the siege
Replaced frontal assault with blockade, siege works and Dutch naval bombardment, and directed the final storming of Hara Castle.
Remained one of the most powerful officials of the shogunate.

conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/casualties: Most deaths were among the defenders of Hara Castle, whom contemporary and modern estimates put at about 27,000 to 37,000, including many women and children; almost all were killed in or after the final assault. Shogunal losses in killed and wounded were also heavy, reported in Japanese records as several thousand to over 10,000 casualties, but the proportion killed is uncertain.
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/effects/0: The shogunate expelled the Portuguese in 1639 and confined the Dutch to Dejima in 1641, completing Japan's policy of restricted foreign contact.
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/effects/1: Temple registration and annual certification that households were not Christian became universal, binding every Japanese family to a Buddhist temple.
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/effects/2: The Shimabara peninsula, largely depopulated, was resettled with migrants from other regions.
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/effects/3: The rebellion reinforced the shogunate's view of Christianity as a subversive foreign creed for more than two centuries.
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/effectsOnC: Open Christianity in Japan was destroyed, and the faith survived only among hidden Christians (Kakure Kirishitan) without priests until the 1860s.
Rewards for denouncing Christians and the systematic use of fumie made secret Christian life extremely dangerous.
The Catholic Church did not include the rebels among Japan's beatified martyrs, distinguishing armed resistance from martyrdom.
In Europe, Catholic writers cited the Dutch bombardment as evidence of Protestant complicity in persecution.
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/legacy: The Shimabara Rebellion closed the 'Christian century' in Japan. For the Tokugawa it justified a policy of eradication and isolation; for Japanese Christians it became a painful memory of faith, desperation and slaughter. Novels, films and popular culture have made Amakusa Shirō an emblem of doomed rebellion, while historians continue to debate how far the revolt was a peasant uprising and how far a Christian holy war.
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/dissenters: Japanese Catholic teaching under persecution, spread through lay confraternities and the martyrdom manuals of the Jesuits, urged believers to endure suffering and die for the faith rather than take up arms; many Christian communities, including those around Nagasaki, did not join the rising.
Whether from conviction or self-preservation, the rebel painter urged negotiation and secretly sought terms with the besiegers, later claiming that he had opposed the course of the rising.
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/theatres/0: Arima and Kuchinotsu, outbreak of the rising
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/theatres/4: Siege and massacre of Hara Castle
conflicts/shimabara-rebellion/campaigns/: The Amakusa insurgents' march to Hara
Amakusa villagers and rōnin under Amakusa Shirō

After defeating Terazawa forces near Hondo and failing to take Tomioka Castle, the Amakusa rebels crossed the strait to the Shimabara peninsula and joined the Shimabara insurgents in the ruined Hara Castle.
Sent from Edo to take over the campaign, Nobutsuna travelled west to Kyushu and arrived at Hara as Itakura's assaults failed, taking command of an army drawn from the Kyushu domains.
